Your Code of Conduct Does Not Cover AI: Why Boards Need a Digital Ethics Framework Now

A rulebook written for human decisions needs a way to test digital decisions too.

Pupsi Phull · Phull Insights22 September 20262 min readGovernance & Technology
Evidence boundary

Personal analysis and professional reflection based on earlier postgraduate work. Named-company examples describe historical research, not current 2026 corporate policies, figures or commitments. No unpublished case result is represented as a verified outcome.

Why this matters

Automation can affect recruitment, performance management and customer decisions. A general commitment to fairness is useful, but it does not by itself assign responsibility for reviewing a specific use case.

What the evidence suggests

The historical DHL-themed governance proposal behind this article used three lenses: duties to people, the character of the organisation, and the likely consequences of a decision. These lenses expose questions that a technical deployment checklist may miss.

What it looks like in practice

A cross-functional review can ask what data a tool needs, who may be disadvantaged, how a person can challenge an outcome, and which accountable leader can stop or amend the use. Legal compliance remains essential, but the ethical question may be wider.

Practical next steps

Three things leaders can do now

01

Map tools that monitor, profile or influence decisions about people.

02

Give each use case an accountable owner and a route for challenge.

03

Review the human impact before rollout and again when the use changes.

Phull Insights Perspective

The view beneath the headline.

Digital ethics works best as a decision practice, not a decorative policy. The test is whether a difficult use case can be slowed down, questioned and changed.
